summary.title: How modern browsers work
summary.one_liner: You learn how a modern browser turns a URL into pixels, from networking and HTML/CSS/JS parsing through layout, painting and GPU compositing, with Chromium as the main example.
takeaways: Every navigation starts in the browser process, which hands network fetching to a separate network service and keeps renderers isolated for security.
HTML parsing builds the DOM incrementally, the preload scanner fetches sub-resources ahead of the parser, and parser-blocking scripts pause parsing unless marked async or defer.
Stylesheets are turned into a CSSOM and combined with the DOM to compute styles, which then drive layout and painting.
Painting records drawing commands that are split into layers and tiles, then rasterized on worker threads and composited on the GPU, so animations can avoid full repaints.
Developer advice such as using defer/async, minimizing forced layout, and using preload or Fetch Priority follows directly from these internals.
summary.summary: The article is a developer-oriented overview of browser internals, focused on Chromium (Blink, V8, Skia) with notes on how Gecko and WebKit differ. It walks through the pipeline in order: networking and resource loading (DNS, TLS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, redirects, MIME checks), then HTML/CSS/JS parsing into the DOM and CSSOM, then style, layout, painting, and compositing on the GPU. It explains practical implications for performance, such as render-blocking CSS, script blocking, speculative loading, and layout cost. The page text is cut off partway through the section on rasterization with Skia.
